edges.description: The loss of regenerable GSH leaves hemoglobin and membrane proteins undefended against reactive oxygen species.
Oxidatively injured, poorly deformable erythrocytes are hemolyzed, especially after an oxidant trigger such as fava bean ingestion.
Premature destruction of oxidatively vulnerable erythrocytes produces hemolytic anemia.
Fava bean ingestion is the documented oxidant trigger of acute hemolysis in this disorder.

Severe neonatal jaundice was the presenting feature of a GR-deficient patient; that it results from hemolysis in the newborn period is inferred from the enzyme defect, since the report states only the jaundice.
Oxidative injury to lens fiber cells manifests as cataract.
Impaired glutathione-dependent defense is reflected in abnormal phagocyte oxidative physiology.

edges.limitations: The mouse shows a clear host-defense defect after massive bacterial challenge, whereas clinically significant immunodeficiency has not been reported in GR-deficient patients; only abnormal neutrophil oxygen consumption was described in the index family.

The mouse allele is a chemically induced mutation at the Gr1 locus, not a human GSR variant, and leaves about 2% residual activity where the human enzyme-null patients have essentially none. The study measured erythrocyte indices only without an oxidant challenge, so it says nothing about oxidant-triggered hemolysis.

nodes.description: With the GSH antioxidant buffer depleted, oxidant exposure denatures hemoglobin and damages the erythrocyte membrane, reducing cell integrity and marking the cell for removal. The reserve capacity of GR in normal red cells is large, so impaired GSH recovery under oxidant stress emerges only when enzyme activity is almost completely lost.

nodes.description: Without GR, erythrocytes cannot reduce GSSG back to GSH after an oxidant challenge, so the reduced-glutathione pool collapses under oxidative stress. Baseline GSH may appear near-normal because little is consumed at rest, but glutathione stability during an oxidant challenge is severely diminished.

nodes.description: Biallelic GSR variants abolish glutathione-disulfide reductase activity. GR is the NADPH- and FAD-dependent flavoenzyme that reduces oxidized glutathione disulfide (GSSG) back to reduced glutathione (GSH). In affected erythrocytes and leukocytes the enzyme protein is unstable or undetectable and GR activity is essentially absent and cannot be restored by FAD in vitro or by riboflavin in vivo, distinguishing the genetic defect from acquired FAD-undersaturation.

nodes.description: A chemically induced glutathione reductase mutant at the Gr1 structural locus on mouse chromosome 8. Homozygotes retain about 2% of normal blood GR activity, with the loss present in blood and other tissues. Without an oxidant challenge their erythrocyte indices are normal, as baseline red-cell GSH is normal in GR-deficient patients; triggered hemolysis was not tested.

nodes.description: Because GR is also deficient in leukocytes, glutathione-dependent antioxidant and bactericidal function of phagocytes is impaired. In the propositus, polymorphonuclear cells showed abnormal oxygen consumption after phagocytosis, suggesting a role for the GR reaction in the bactericidal capacity of these cells. This is an observation in a single family and the clinical significance of the leukocyte defect is not established.

evidence.reference_title: Glutathione reductase facilitates host defense by sustaining phagocytic oxidative burst and promoting the development of neutrophil extracellular traps.
evidence.snippet: Unlike wild-type neutrophils that exhibited a sustained oxidative burst upon stimulation with phorbol ester and fMLP, Gsr-deficient neutrophils displayed a very transient oxidative burst that abruptly ceased shortly after stimulation.

nodes.description: The thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase system can reduce GSSG to GSH and acts as a functional backup for GR. In Gsr-knockout mice, inner-ear thioredoxin and thioredoxin reductase activities rose and no oxidative damage or hearing deficit developed. This compensation is a candidate explanation for why hemolysis in the human disorder has been reported after oxidant triggers, but it has not been measured in GR-deficient patients, and any dampening effect on hemolysis is hypothesized rather than shown.
